title: Borderline: an emotional spike and its slow return
description: Something emotionally upsetting happens. The episode follows the response in a brain with borderline personality disorder; the typical response shows the same moment in a brain without it. What stands out most in the research is not where the response happens but how it unfolds in time: the response is slower to come back down, and it does not fade with repetition the way it usually does.
caveat: This is the least settled of the four episodes, and every region in it is marked as mixed or debated. Two pooled analyses disagree about whether the amygdala is more or less active, and the largest and most recent one found no consistent pattern at all across studies. The slow return to baseline comes from single studies, in which people looked at upsetting pictures in a scanner for seconds to minutes. Nothing here measures the hours that an episode can last in life, and upsetting pictures are a weak stand-in for the interpersonal events that usually set an episode off. Most participants in these studies were women, and medication appears to change the findings.

phases.name: Something upsetting
phases.caption: Something emotionally upsetting happens. In the studies behind this episode, that is an upsetting picture.
phases.typicalCaption: Something emotionally upsetting happens. In the studies behind this episode, that is an upsetting picture.

phases.name: Surge
phases.caption: The emotional response builds. The insula and the posterior cingulate respond more than in a typical brain, and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, a control region, responds less. Whether the amygdala responds more or less is disputed, so it is drawn the same as in a typical brain at this step.
phases.typicalCaption: The emotional response builds. The amygdala and the anterior cingulate respond, as they do to anything upsetting.

order.rationale: The pooled analyses compare overall response to upsetting versus neutral pictures and say nothing about what comes first. Placing the surge straight after the trigger follows the design of those tasks.

phases.name: Not settling
phases.caption: Where a typical response would start to fade, this one holds. The amygdala is slower to return to its resting level, and seeing the same thing again does not dull the response.
phases.typicalCaption: The response starts to fade. With repetition the dorsal anterior cingulate becomes more active, the insula and amygdala work more closely together, and the amygdala settles.

citations.authors: Hazlett EA, Zhang J, New AS, Zelmanova Y, Goldstein KE, Haznedar MM, Meyerson D, Goodman M, Siever LJ, Chu KW
citations.title: Potentiated amygdala response to repeated emotional pictures in borderline personality disorder.
citations.quote: the BPD patients exhibited an overall amygdala BOLD response curve (averaged across all repeated-measures except Time) with a much slower return to baseline compared with the HC and SPD groups

phases.name: Slow return
phases.caption: The response comes down slowly. Scans have only followed this for minutes; how it continues over the hours an episode can last has not been measured.
phases.typicalCaption: The response has largely settled, and the ventromedial prefrontal cortex has become more active.

order.rationale: Studies show the amygdala response not decreasing over the minutes of a task. That it eventually comes down, and how, is an assumption; no study read for this episode followed it to the end.

regions.explanation: The most disputed finding. One pooled analysis found the left amygdala more active than in people without the condition, mainly in people not taking medication. Another found it less active. The largest found no consistent difference. What single studies do show is a difference in timing: the response is slower to return to baseline and does not shrink when the same upsetting picture is shown again. Because the size of the response is disputed, it is drawn rising to the same height as in the typical brain; only the slower return differs.
